kurz: How to work back from the share price to what the market already expects of a company, and then check only this one number instead of the company's value.

bloecke.md:
Every forward valuation has the same fundamental flaw. It ends with a number that the person doing the calculation has chosen themselves through their assumptions. An analyst who likes a company assumes 12% growth instead of 8% and 8% cost of capital instead of 10%. The result is then the one they had suspected beforehand. A sensitivity table makes the problem visible but does not solve it, because it only offers a larger selection of results from which you can pick the one you want.

The share price, by contrast, is the only quantity in the model that is not your own assumption. A reverse DCF takes it as given and rearranges the equation. Instead of asking what the company is worth, you ask what would have to happen for today's price to be right. Instead of a valuation, the result is the expectation contained in today's price. Such an expectation can be checked against reality, whereas a forecast can only be believed.

bloecke.erklaerung: The equation is the same as in the ordinary DCF model. It differs only in which quantity is known. In the reverse DCF, the enterprise value EV on the left is given, and the growth rate g is the unknown.
variablen: enterprise value = market capitalisation + net financial debt + minority interests and pensions − non-operating assets
free cash flow of the base period, preferably a multi-year average rather than a single year
growth in phase 1 that is solved for (the one unknown)
cost of capital (WACC), set by the analyst
perpetual growth from year n+1, set by the analyst
length of the growth phase in years
bloecke.beispiel: 30 billion = f(g) with FCF0 = 500 million, w = 9%, ge = 2%, n = 10  →  g = 21% p.a.

bloecke.md:
## One unknown per calculation

The equation contains several free variables, of which only one can be backed out at a time. Which one you choose depends on the company.

- With **implied growth**, the cost of capital, margin and perpetual growth are fixed. The growth rate of phase 1 is changed until the present value equals the enterprise value derived from the market capitalisation. This is the normal case for profitable companies.
- The **implied margin** is suitable for firms that grow but barely earn anything. For them, growth is the easier assumption. You therefore specify revenue growth and look for the operating margin that justifies the share price. You then need to check, for example, whether any company in this industry has ever achieved a 25% EBIT margin.
- With the **implied duration of the competitive advantage**, growth and margin are held at today's level. The unknown is n, that is, the number of years with excess returns that the share price assumes. Rappaport and Mauboussin popularised this reading in *Expectations Investing*.

The solution is found by trial and error rather than analytically. You enter a value, read off the present value and adjust. Any spreadsheet or DCF calculator does this in a few minutes.

A company generates €500 million of free cash flow, has no net financial debt and is valued at €30 billion, that is, at 60 times FCF. This is not an extreme case, because for January 2026 Damodaran reports an EV/EBIT of 32.4 for the US software industry, and 44.3 for semiconductors with a trailing P/E of 100.2.

The assumptions are a 9% cost of capital (KPMG reports an average of 9.4% for Technology), a growth phase of ten years and perpetual growth of 2% thereafter. The unknown is the growth rate at which the sum of the present values comes to exactly €30 billion.

The calculation gives 21% growth a year over ten years. For this, free cash flow would have to rise from €500 million to €3.36 billion, that is, to 6.7 times its current level. Even then, 69% of today's market capitalisation is still attributable to the terminal value, that is, to the assumption that the cash flow keeps growing at 2% forever after year ten.

bloecke.titel: Growth assumption and enterprise value (illustrative calculation, WACC 9%, perpetual growth 2%)
Enterprise value for each assumed growth rate
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with FCF of €500 million, WACC of 9% and perpetual growth of 2%; the market capitalisation of €30 billion lies between the 20% and the 25% assumption, at exactly 21%.

bloecke.md:
This changes the task. Instead of estimating the company's value, you only have to judge whether 21% cash flow growth over ten years is more likely than not. This judgement rests on base rates rather than opinions. Questions to clarify include how large the addressable market is if the cash flow increases almost sevenfold, how many competitors would have to disappear for that to happen, and how many companies with this profile have achieved something like this in the past.

The empirical findings on this are not very encouraging. Company growth is only weakly persistent, and beyond three to five years growth forecasts contain little information. This does not count against the share, because high growth rates do occur. It does mean, however, that the share price contains a statement that is rarely true, and that you know this statement before you buy.

In addition, the implied expectation reacts only weakly to changes in the price. If the price falls from €30 billion to €19.2 billion, that is, by 36%, the implied growth rate only falls from 21% to 15%. A price drop of a third therefore lowers the expectation by six percentage points. This is due to the compounding effect in phase 1, which means that even a few percentage points of growth account for a lot of value.

bloecke.titel: Implied growth at an unchanged share price under different assumptions
bloecke.unter: With the same market capitalisation of €30 billion and the same cash flow base, one point more WACC requires around two and a half points more growth, and one point more perpetual growth around one and a half points less; figures in % p.a.

bloecke.md:
The result does not show the market's expectation, but the expectation that your own model attributes to the market. Three inputs shift the result before the company itself even comes into play.

The cost of capital is an estimate, not a measurement. The range in the matrix above shows how strongly the result depends on it.

As for the cash flow base, a single year without investment or with a reduction in working capital leads to a one-off high FCF and therefore to an implied growth rate that is far too low. If share-based payment is also excluded, the base is systematically set too high. Under IFRS 2, this remuneration must be recognised as an expense at fair value. Although it is non-cash, it genuinely dilutes the shareholders' stakes.

As for the number of shares, the diluted share count is what matters. A company that pays for part of its growth in shares has to spread the value over more shares than are outstanding today.

## Reverse DCF for the overall market

Damodaran's implied market risk premium is a reverse DCF on the S&P 500. The index level is given, dividends and buybacks are projected forward, and the unknown is the interest rate at which the present value of these distributions equals the index level. As of 1 September 2026, this gives a premium of 4.14% over a risk-free rate of 4.75%. Together, that is an expected nominal return of around 8.9% in dollars before tax. In the previous month, the premium was 4.28%. Depending on the cash flow definition, the same source reports a premium between 3.56% and 6.05%. For the overall market, too, the result is a range rather than an exact value.

The historical record shows a relationship that a look at multiples does not reveal. Since 1990, the expected total return has mostly fluctuated between 7% and 9%. What shifts above all is the split between interest rate and premium. At the end of 1990, two thirds of the total return consisted of the risk-free rate; at the end of 2020, more than four fifths consisted of the premium. At the end of 2020, the total expectation was only 5.65%, the lowest value in the series.

bloecke.titel: Expected return priced in by the US market (year-end values)
bloecke.unter: The sum of the risk-free rate and the implied risk premium is the expected return priced in by the market. Source: Damodaran, histimpl.

bloecke.md:
For the cost of capital, German valuation practice follows the IDW S1 standard. What matters there is a risk-free base rate (Basiszins) derived from the Bundesbank's Svensson yield curve and calculated as a three-month average, not the current day's yield on the German federal bond (3.52% on 18 September 2026). The KPMG Cost of Capital Study 2025 reports an average WACC of 8.5% and a cost of equity of 9.7%, but it uses a base rate of 2.5%. At the interest rate level of 2026, the cost of capital is likely to be higher, which raises the implied growth rates purely mathematically.

The income tax burden of a German corporation is made up of 15% corporation tax under Section 23(1) KStG (Corporation Tax Act), a 5.5% solidarity surcharge on it, and trade tax (Gewerbesteuer), which is the assessment rate (Steuermesszahl) of 3.5% under Section 11(2) GewStG (Trade Tax Act) multiplied by the municipal multiplier (Hebesatz). In municipalities with 20,000 or more inhabitants, multipliers in 2025 were between 250% and 580%, which put the total burden at around 24.6% to 36.1%. Berlin, Frankfurt and Munich come to 30.2%, 31.9% and 33.0%. Since July 2025, Section 23(1) KStG has laid down that corporation tax will fall to 14% from 2028 and then by one point a year to 10% from 2032. If this lowers the total burden from around 31% to around 25.7%, after-tax profit rises by about 7.7% for this reason alone. Spread over five years, that is around one and a half points of annual growth for which no additional customer has to be won. A reverse calculation with a constant tax rate attributes this effect to the operating business. In municipalities with a low multiplier, the minimum trade tax multiplier, which rises from 200% to 280% from 2027 (Section 16(4) GewStG), works in the opposite direction.

On the investor side, the 8.9% priced in by the US market applies before tax. On income above the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 under Section 20(9) EStG (Income Tax Act), a German private investor pays 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) under Section 32d(1) EStG plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge on it under Section 4 SolzG 1995 (Solidarity Surcharge Act), together 26.375%. This rate applies to individual shares. For an equity ETF, 30% of the income is tax-free under the partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) in Section 20(1) InvStG (Investment Tax Act), which lowers the burden to around 18.5% of the income. The return expectation contained in the share price is therefore not what ultimately reaches the investor.

schritte.titel: Convert the price into enterprise value
schritte.text: Add net financial debt, minority interests and pension obligations to the market capitalisation and deduct non-operating assets. Without this step, you are comparing equity with total capital.
Use a multi-year average instead of a record year, treat share-based payment as an expense and record lease payments under IFRS 16 consistently. Write down the definition chosen.
Note the WACC, perpetual growth and length of phase 1 before the calculation, not afterwards when the result is already known.
Change growth, margin or duration until the present value equals the enterprise value determined in the first step.
Check market size, industry growth, capital requirements, competition and the historical frequency of such rates. The insight comes from this step, not from the calculation.
Repeat the calculation with two other WACC values. The result is a range of implied expectations, and only this range is a reliable statement.

links.titel: Backwards from the price to the expectation
punkte: The fixed quantity, the share price, is the starting point and not a benchmark for comparison
The result can be checked, because 21% over ten years is a statement about reality
Less prone to confirmation bias, because the result cannot be set to suit your wishes
Works without a forecast of your own and therefore also for companies outside your own circle of competence

rechts.titel: Forwards from the forecast to the value
punkte: Provides a target value that you can seemingly act on
All inputs are set by yourself, so the result follows your own expectation
The seemingly precise result hides the uncertainty of the inputs
Indispensable when there is no market price, for example in a company acquisition, a compensation payment or the division of an estate

bloecke.md: The reverse DCF does not answer a valuation question. It makes visible what has to happen for today's share price to be justified. Your own work then consists only of judging how often something like that happens.

mitnehmen: In the reverse DCF, the share price is the given quantity and growth is the unknown, so the most arbitrary assumption of the classic DCF disappears.
In the illustrative calculation, a market capitalisation of €30 billion with €500 million of free cash flow, a 9% WACC and 2% perpetual growth implies annual cash flow growth of 21% over ten years.
The implied figure depends on your own assumptions (one point more WACC requires around two and a half points more growth) and should therefore always be reported as a range, never as a point value.
The implied market risk premium applies the same method to an index and stood at 4.14% over a 4.75% risk-free rate as of September 2026, together an expected nominal return of around 8.9% before tax.
A cash flow base that is too high (record year, share-based payment excluded, undiluted share count) makes the expectation contained in the share price appear lower than it is.

begriffe.text: Reversal of the present value calculation. The share price is taken as given, and the unknown is the assumption (usually growth) that justifies it. The result is the expectation contained in the price, not a valuation.

Growth rate of the cash flows at which the present value of a valuation model exactly equals the current market price. It depends on the other assumptions and should therefore always be stated as a range.

Excess return of equities over the risk-free rate, backed out from the index level and expected distributions, that is, a reverse DCF at market level. As of September 2026, Damodaran reported 4.14% for the S&P 500.

Number of shares including all subscription rights, convertible bonds and share-based payments that can lead to new shares. Only this figure is suitable for converting a company value into a value per share.
